opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the field is still really pre-paradigmatic. We don't have a settled understanding of what the hardest parts of the alignment problem are going to turn out to be, or which research directions will actually bear fruit as systems get more capable. If you look across thoughtful researchers, you see deep, persistent disagreement about basic questions: how fast capabilities will advance, whether techniques that work on today's models will generalize, and whether the main risk comes from deceptive misalignment, misuse, or something more diffuse. When the experts themselves are this split, it would be pretty overconfident for a funder to pick one horse and go all in.

There's also a practical asymmetry. If we waited until we had highly confident views before funding anything, we'd be sitting on our hands during exactly the period when building up the field matters most. A lot of the value of early grants is in creating the people, the institutions, and the empirical results that let everyone, including us, form better views. So funding a portfolio is partly how we learn. You fund interpretability, scalable oversight, evals, adversarial robustness, governance-adjacent work, and then you watch what produces real traction and update.

And I'd say it's not that we have no views. We do have opinions, and they shape the weighting. But I think there's a kind of humility that's appropriate when you're a large funder in a small field. Your bets can end up defining what the field even works on. If we concentrated everything on our own best guess and that guess was wrong, we could set the whole field back in a way that's hard to recover from. Spreading across approaches is a hedge against our own blind spots, and it keeps the ecosystem diverse enough that good ideas we didn't anticipate can actually get a hearing.

r001.rationale: The candidate says waiting for highly confident views before funding would mean sitting out a period when building the field matters, capturing delayed grantmaking as a cost of developing confidence.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes persistent disagreement among researchers, but does not say that substantial investigation would still leave reasonable competing views.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not mention relying on advisors to diversify grants or argue that diversification would remain the choice after detailed internal investigation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest starting point is that the question of what's actually going to make transformative AI go well is just a really hard, unsettled question. There's a lot of smart people who've thought about it for a long time and still disagree pretty fundamentally, both about the shape of the risks and about what kinds of work actually reduce them. Some people think the core problem is alignment in a fairly technical sense, some think it's governance and coordination, some think the biggest lever is interpretability or evaluations or just slowing things down. And I don't think any of those camps has a knockdown case.

So given that, there's a version of a funder that says, "we're going to sit down, figure out the right answer, and then fund only that." And I think that's actually a pretty fragile strategy. If you're a large funder and you concentrate heavily on one theory of change, and that theory turns out to be wrong, you've not only wasted money, you've potentially shaped the whole field around a mistaken view, because your funding decisions change what people work on and what careers look viable. Our views really do have outsized influence on the ecosystem, so being wrong in a correlated, confident way is a lot worse than being wrong in a hedged way.

The other thing is that there's real value in the field itself generating the information you'd need to form confident views. A lot of what we learn about which approaches are promising comes from actually trying them. If you fund mechanistic interpretability for a few years and it either produces real traction or it stalls out, that teaches you something you couldn't have reasoned your way to from an armchair. So in some sense, spreading bets is part of how you eventually earn the right to have more confident views. It's an exploration strategy, not just a hedge.

Now, I want to be careful here, because "fund a diversity of approaches" can become an excuse for not having views at all, and I don't think that's right either. We do have views, and they do inform where we lean. We think some things are more promising than others, and we try to say so. But there's a difference between having a probability distribution over what matters and collapsing that distribution to a point. The distribution is still pretty wide for us, and I think it should be, and the grantmaking should reflect that width rather than pretending to a certainty we don't actually have.

And then the last piece is just that the field is small and young enough that the marginal value of having more people working on roughly reasonable things is still high. In a more mature field you'd expect more of the value to come from picking winners. Here I think a lot of the value still comes from growing the pool of serious, capable people who are oriented toward the problem at all, and you don't need to have resolved the big strategic disagreements to see that that's worth doing.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes waiting to settle on one theory before funding, but does not clearly identify delayed grantmaking as an opportunity cost of building detailed internal views.

r002.rationale: It says smart people have thought about the issue for a long time and still disagree fundamentally about risks and which work reduces them.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention relying on advisors to diversify grants or argue that this could shortcut Open Philanthropy’s internal view-building.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic reason is that we’re making decisions under a lot of uncertainty, and we shouldn’t expect to resolve all of that uncertainty before funding useful work. There are disagreements about what advanced AI systems will look like, what the biggest risks will be, and which approaches could actually help. Developing a very confident view on all of those questions is itself a substantial research project.

And funding research is one of the ways you learn. You can support people pursuing different approaches, see what progress they make, and use that to inform future decisions. If you require yourself to know which approach is right before you fund anything, you can end up preventing the work that would help you figure that out.

That doesn’t mean spreading money evenly across every proposal. You still need judgments about whether an approach has a plausible case, whether the people working on it are strong, and whether additional funding would be useful. But you can have enough confidence to think, ‘This is worth trying,’ without having enough confidence to think, ‘This is the approach that’s going to solve the problem.’

r001.rationale: It says developing a confident view is a substantial research project and warns that waiting to know which approach is right can prevent useful work, identifying the opportunity cost of delayed grants.

r002.rationale: It describes uncertainty and disagreement but does not say that substantial investigation would still leave reasonable competing views.

r003.rationale: It recommends funding different approaches to learn, but does not say Open Philanthropy can rely on advisors to diversify grants or that diversification would likely remain its choice after internal investigation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that we're operating in a field where there's a lot of uncertainty, and it's pretty hard to resolve that uncertainty just by thinking harder before you fund anything. People have different pictures of what advanced AI systems will look like, what will make them dangerous, and what kinds of research could help. You can find thoughtful researchers pursuing quite different approaches without having a decisive argument that one of them is right.

So I don't think a funder needs to first solve all of those disagreements. Part of what you're buying with a grant is information: you give someone the resources to pursue an idea, and then you can see whether it produces useful results. If you insist on being highly confident beforehand, you risk only funding things that fit your existing worldview, and missing an approach that turns out to be important.

That doesn't mean spreading money indiscriminately. You still want a plausible story for how the work could help, capable people doing it, and some way to learn from how it goes. But I think there's a reasonable division of labor where researchers pursue their particular bets, and we support a portfolio while continuing to refine our own views.

r001.rationale: The response says it is hard to resolve uncertainty before funding and that waiting for confidence risks missing important approaches, but it does not clearly identify delayed grantmaking as the opportunity cost of developing detailed internal views.

r002.rationale: It says thinking harder before funding is unlikely to resolve the uncertainty and that thoughtful researchers pursue different approaches without a decisive argument for one, conveying that reasonable competing views would remain.

r003.rationale: The response describes supporting a portfolio while refining internal views, but does not say Open Philanthropy can rely on advisors to diversify grants or that investigation would likely leave diversification as its choice.
